_comment: Academy glossary. Key = the exact token as it appears in the text (case-sensitive, plural 's' is matched automatically). Value = [expansion, one-sentence explanation]. Read by assets/js/study.js, which marks the first occurrence of each term in every section with a click-to-reveal definition. Keep explanations to one plain sentence.
API: The contract a piece of software exposes so other programs can call it, for example the HTTP endpoints of a service.
REST: A style of HTTP API where resources have URLs and the standard verbs GET, POST, PUT and DELETE act on them.
HTTP: The request-and-response protocol browsers and services use to talk over the web.
HTTPS: HTTP carried over an encrypted TLS connection, so nobody on the path can read or alter the traffic.
HTTP/2: A binary, multiplexed revision of HTTP that sends many requests over one connection at once.
HTTP/3: The newest HTTP revision, carried over QUIC instead of TCP for faster connection setup.
QUIC: A transport protocol on top of UDP with built-in encryption and fewer round trips than TCP.
TCP: The reliable, ordered byte-stream transport most internet traffic runs on.
UDP: A lightweight transport that sends packets without delivery guarantees, used where speed beats reliability.
TLS: The encryption layer behind HTTPS that protects data in transit and proves the server's identity.
mTLS: TLS where both sides present certificates, so the client is authenticated as well as the server.
SSL: The predecessor of TLS; the name survives in tools and config keys, but modern systems use TLS.
DNS: The directory that turns a host name such as janaka.me into an IP address.
IP: The addressing scheme that routes packets between machines; an IP address identifies one network interface.
URL: A web address: scheme, host, path and optional query, for example https://janaka.me/academy/.
URI: The general form of an identifier for a resource; every URL is a URI.
JSON: A lightweight text format for structured data, the usual payload of web APIs.
YAML: An indentation-based text format for configuration files, used by Docker Compose, Kubernetes and CI pipelines.
XML: A tag-based text format for structured documents, still common in Maven, SOAP and legacy integrations.
CSV: A plain-text table format where each line is a row and commas separate the columns.
UTF: A family of Unicode encodings; UTF-8 is the default on the web and in most modern tools.
HTML: The markup language that describes the structure of a web page.
CSS: The language that describes how HTML elements look: layout, colour, typography.
DOM: The in-memory tree the browser builds from HTML, which scripts read and change.
SPA: A web app that loads one HTML page and updates the view with JavaScript instead of full page reloads.
PWA: A web app that can be installed, work offline and send notifications by using a service worker and a manifest.
SSR: Producing the HTML on the server for each request so the page paints before any JavaScript runs.
CDN: A network of edge servers that caches static files close to the user.
SEO: Making pages easier for search engines to crawl, understand and rank.
UI: The part of a system the user sees and interacts with.
UX: How it feels to use a product end to end, beyond the individual screens.
WCAG: The W3C standard that defines how accessible web content must be, in levels A, AA and AAA.
ARIA: HTML attributes that tell assistive technology what a custom element is and what state it is in.
JDK: The toolset for building Java programs: compiler, runtime, and tools like jshell and jcmd.
JRE: The runtime part of the JDK, enough to run Java programs but not to compile them.
JVM: The runtime that executes compiled Java bytecode and manages memory and threads.
JIT: Compiling hot bytecode to native machine code while the program runs, which is how the JVM gets fast.
AOT: Compiling to native code before the program runs, as GraalVM native images do, for instant startup.
GC: The JVM's automatic reclaiming of memory that is no longer referenced.
G1: The default JVM garbage collector since Java 9, which balances throughput and pause times.
ZGC: A low-latency JVM collector designed for very large heaps with pauses well under a millisecond.
JFR: A low-overhead profiler built into the JDK that records what the JVM was doing.
JMX: A standard for exposing runtime metrics and management operations from a Java process.
JNI: The bridge that lets Java code call native C or C++ libraries.
LTS: A release that receives security and bug fixes for years, such as Java 17, 21 and 25.
EE: The set of enterprise Java specifications, now Jakarta EE, covering servlets, persistence, messaging and more.
JPA: The standard Java API for mapping objects to relational tables, implemented by Hibernate.
JDBC: The low-level Java API for sending SQL to a database and reading the results.
ORM: A library that maps classes to tables so you work with objects instead of raw SQL.
JMS: The standard Java API for sending messages through a broker such as ActiveMQ.
DTO: A plain class that carries data across a boundary, typically the shape of an API request or response.
POJO: An ordinary Java class with no framework dependencies.
IO: Reading and writing data outside the process: files, sockets, databases.
NIO: Java's non-blocking I/O API for channels, buffers and selectors.
MVC: A pattern that separates data (model), presentation (view) and request handling (controller).
CRUD: The four basic operations on stored data, and the shape of most simple APIs.
SQL: The language for querying and changing relational databases.
OLTP: A database workload of many small, fast reads and writes, like an order system.
OLAP: A database workload of large, read-heavy queries for reporting and analysis.
ACID: The guarantees a database transaction gives: all or nothing, valid, isolated from others, and permanent once committed.
AWR: Oracle's built-in store of performance statistics, used for tuning reports.
ADDM: Oracle's analysis tool that reads AWR data and suggests fixes.
TKPROF: Oracle's tool that turns raw SQL trace files into readable performance reports.
ETL: Pulling data from sources, reshaping it and loading it into a target such as a warehouse.
CDC: Streaming every insert, update and delete from a database as events, for example with Debezium.
DLQ: A holding queue for messages that could not be processed, so they are kept instead of lost.
CQRS: Using separate models for writes (commands) and reads (queries).
DDD: Designing software around the business domain and its language, with bounded contexts and aggregates.
EDA: Services that communicate by publishing and reacting to events rather than calling each other directly.
SOA: The earlier style of splitting systems into services, usually with an enterprise service bus in the middle.
ADR: A short document that captures one design decision, its context and its consequences.
RFC: A numbered internet standards document, such as RFC 9110 for HTTP; also used for internal design proposals.
SLO: A target for a reliability measure, for example 99.9 % of requests under 300 ms.
SLA: A contractual promise about service quality, usually backed by penalties.
SLI: The measured quantity behind an SLO, such as error rate or latency.
MTTR: The average time from an incident starting to the service working again.
p95: The value below which 95 % of measurements fall; a p95 latency of 300 ms means one request in twenty is slower.
p99: The value below which 99 % of measurements fall, a common tail-latency target.
CI: Automatically building and testing every change as soon as it is pushed.
CD: Automatically taking every green build to a releasable state, or all the way into production.
CI/CD: The automated pipeline that builds, tests and ships every change.
OCI: The standard for container images and runtimes that Docker, Podman and Kubernetes share.
K8s: The container orchestrator that schedules, scales and restarts workloads across a cluster.
VM: A software-emulated computer with its own operating system, running on a physical host.
IaC: Describing servers, networks and services in versioned files, applied by tools like Terraform.
SBOM: A machine-readable list of every library and version inside a build, used for vulnerability checks.
CVE: The public identifier for a known security vulnerability, such as CVE-2021-44228.
SAST: Scanning source code for security flaws without running it.
DAST: Probing a running application for security flaws from the outside.
SCA: Checking the third-party dependencies of a build for known vulnerabilities and licence issues.
PII: Any data that can identify a person, which must be handled under privacy law.
GDPR: The EU privacy law that governs how personal data is collected and processed.
SSH: The encrypted protocol for logging into remote machines and running commands.
SFTP: File transfer that runs over an SSH connection.
SCP: Copying files between hosts over SSH.
CLI: A program you drive by typing commands in a terminal.
IDE: An editor with build, debug and refactoring tools built in, such as IntelliJ or VS Code.
OS: The software layer that manages hardware and runs programs: Linux, Windows, macOS.
WSL: A Linux environment that runs inside Windows.
CPU: The processor that executes instructions; CPU time is the usual measure of compute cost.
RAM: The fast working memory of a machine, cleared when it powers off.
SSD: Flash-based storage with no moving parts, much faster than a spinning disk.
NUMA: A multi-socket design where memory attached to another CPU is slower to reach.
S3: Amazon's object storage, and the de-facto API that MinIO and others implement.
IAM: The service or component that defines who may do what in a system.
RBAC: Granting permissions to roles and assigning roles to users.
SSO: Logging in once and being recognised by many applications.
MFA: Requiring a second proof of identity, such as a one-time code, in addition to a password.
OAuth: The standard for letting one application act on a user's behalf at another without sharing the password.
OAuth2: The current version of OAuth, the basis of most modern login and API authorisation flows.
OIDC: An identity layer on top of OAuth2 that tells the application who the user is.
PKCE: An OAuth2 extension that protects the authorisation code so a public client such as a browser app cannot be hijacked.
JWT: A signed, base64-encoded token that carries claims about a user, typically as a bearer token.
JWKS: The published set of public keys a service uses to verify JWT signatures.
CORS: The browser mechanism that lets a page call an API on another origin, controlled by response headers.
CSRF: An attack that tricks a logged-in browser into sending a request the user did not intend.
CSP: A response header that tells the browser which scripts, styles and resources a page may load.
HSTS: A header that tells browsers to only ever use HTTPS for this host.
XSS: An attack that injects script into a page seen by other users.
MDC: A per-thread map in SLF4J and Logback that adds fields such as a request ID to every log line.
SLF4J: The logging API Java libraries write to, with Logback or Log4j behind it.
APM: Tooling that traces requests through a system and reports latency and errors.
OTel: The vendor-neutral standard and SDKs for traces, metrics and logs.
SSE: A one-way stream of events from server to browser over a single HTTP connection.
gRPC: A high-performance RPC framework using HTTP/2 and Protocol Buffers.
RPC: Calling a function on another machine as if it were local.
MQTT: A lightweight publish-subscribe protocol common in IoT devices.
IoT: Networked physical devices such as sensors and meters.
TTL: How long a cache entry, DNS record or message stays valid before it expires.
LRU: A cache eviction policy that discards the entry not touched for the longest time.
UUID: A 128-bit random or time-based identifier, written as 36 hexadecimal characters with hyphens.
SemVer: The MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH scheme where each part signals breaking, additive or fixing changes.
BOM: In Maven, a POM that pins the versions of a family of libraries so they are consistent.
POM: Maven's pom.xml, which describes a project's coordinates, dependencies and build.
npm: The package manager and registry for JavaScript libraries.
ESM: The standard JavaScript module system with import and export.
TDD: Writing a failing test first, then the code that makes it pass, then refactoring.
BDD: Specifying behaviour in readable given-when-then scenarios before implementing it.
POC: A small build that shows an idea works before investing in the real thing.
MVP: The smallest version of a product that delivers value and can be tested with users.
ISO: The body behind standards such as ISO 8601 dates and ISO 27001 security management.
OKR: A goal-setting method: a qualitative objective with measurable key results.
KPI: A metric chosen to track progress towards a business goal.
ROI: The gain from an investment relative to its cost.
TCO: The full cost of a system over its life: licences, hosting, people and maintenance.
B2B: Selling to companies rather than consumers.
AI: Software that performs tasks that normally need human judgement, today mostly via machine-learning models.
ML: Building models that learn patterns from data instead of following hand-written rules.
LLM: A neural network trained on vast text that generates and understands language, such as Claude or GPT.
GPT: OpenAI's family of large language models.
RAG: Fetching relevant documents first and giving them to the model, so its answers are grounded in your data.
MCP: The open standard that lets an AI application connect to tools, data and prompts through a common server interface.
SDK: The official library and tools for building against a platform or API.
NLP: The field of making software understand and generate human language.
MDM: Keeping one authoritative copy of core business entities such as customers and products.
AAS: An Oracle metric: how many sessions were actively working on average over an interval.
CCAR: The US Federal Reserve's annual stress test of large banks.
AST: The tree a compiler or parser builds to represent the structure of source code.
SIEM: A platform that collects logs across systems to detect and investigate security incidents.
